RC1.title: Beyond the dollar? The politics of local-currency trade
RC1.text: Since the Second World War, the dollar has served as the world's default currency for invoicing trade, pricing commodities, holding reserves and settling debts. Its dominance is so familiar that it has ceased to look like a policy choice at all. Yet the weaponisation of financial plumbing, through sanctions that freeze reserves, cut banks off from messaging networks or restrict access to dollar clearing, has prompted many governments to ask whether so much of their commerce should depend on a currency issued by a rival or a potential adversary. Hence the growing talk of "de-dollarisation": the effort to settle trade in rupees, yuan, dirhams and other local currencies. The motives are easy to understand. Dollar invoicing exposes exporters and importers to exchange-rate swings unrelated to their own economies; when the dollar strengthens, borrowers with dollar debts see their burden rise even if nothing at home has changed. Using local currencies promises to lower transaction costs, shorten settlement chains and, not incidentally, insulate trade from sanctions risk. For countries that buy large volumes of energy from partners who are themselves under sanctions, local-currency settlement can be the only practicable route. But a currency is not merely a unit of account; it is a network, and networks reward incumbency. The dollar's advantage lies less in any single feature than in the combination: deep and liquid financial markets, legal protection for investors, free convertibility, and a vast supply of safe assets in which surplus earnings can be parked. A trading partner who accepts rupees must be able to do something useful with them. If they cannot be spent on goods the issuing country exports, or invested in assets the partner trusts, they pile up as idle balances. Some recent arrangements have struggled on precisely this problem, with exporters holding large sums of a currency they could neither convert freely nor use productively. The imbalance is revealing. Bilateral trade that is roughly balanced can be settled in either currency without much friction; lopsided trade cannot. When a country imports heavily from a partner but exports little to it, settlement in the importer's currency leaves the partner holding ever larger balances that it may be unable to spend or invest, while settlement in the partner's currency forces the importer to find that currency elsewhere. The alternative is a third currency, which brings the dollar straight back in. This is why advocates of local-currency trade increasingly emphasise supporting infrastructure, such as swap lines between central banks, rupee-denominated bonds that foreign holders can buy, and interlinked payment systems, rather than simple declarations of intent. Moreover, convertibility is a double-edged commitment. Opening the capital account to foreign holders of a currency invites investment but also invites flight. Countries that have long managed their exchange rates and restricted capital movements to protect their economies from sudden stops are reluctant to abandon those protections merely to make their currency more attractive abroad. Internationalisation, in other words, demands that a state surrender some of the control that motivated the exercise in the first place. The paradox is that the autonomy sought through de-dollarisation is partly purchased by relinquishing autonomy of another kind. Central banks' reserve behaviour offers a clue. In recent years several have increased their holdings of gold, an asset that is no one's liability and cannot be frozen by any foreign authority. The shift is modest in proportion to total reserves, yet it is revealing: it suggests that prudence about sanctions exposure is shaping portfolios even where governments insist publicly that nothing is changing. Gold, however, earns no interest and is cumbersome to use in payment, so it can serve as insurance but not as a medium of trade. Sceptics of the whole project also note that dominance is self-reinforcing precisely because the alternatives are fragmented. A world of several regional currencies, each with its own settlement systems and rules, may be more resilient to coercion but is also costlier to navigate. Fragmentation raises transaction costs, complicates hedging and weakens the very network benefits that make any currency attractive. The likelier outcome, many economists believe, is gradual diversification at the margin rather than dethronement: a multipolar arrangement in which the dollar remains first among several, but no longer alone. For a country like India, the sensible approach is probably incremental. Expanding the rupee's role in trade with a few partners where flows are balanced and relations stable, building swap lines and deepening domestic bond markets, and adopting the discipline of low inflation and credible institutions are measures that carry value irrespective of geopolitics. A currency earns trust slowly and loses it quickly; declarations cannot substitute for the dull work of making it worth holding.

RC2.title: Seeing is no longer believing: synthetic media and the economics of trust
RC2.text: For well over a century, photographs, audio recordings and video footage have enjoyed a special status as evidence. A fabricated letter might be dismissed as forgery, but a recorded confession carried a different weight: it seemed to capture reality directly rather than describe it. That presumption is now eroding. Generative systems can synthesise a politician's voice, graft one person's face onto another's body, or produce a convincing "news clip" of an event that never took place, at a cost that has fallen from studio budgets to a few minutes on a consumer laptop. The immediate fear is deception: a fabricated recording released on the eve of an election, a forged video of a company chief announcing a fictitious merger, a cloned voice persuading a relative to transfer money. These dangers are real, and several have already materialised on a small scale. Yet scholars of misinformation caution that the larger damage may be indirect. When any recording might be false, genuine recordings lose their force too. This is the so-called "liar's dividend": a wrongdoer caught on tape can simply claim that the tape is synthetic, and in an environment saturated with fakes, enough of the public may be willing to believe him. The technology need not fool everyone; it needs only to supply the doubt. The harms are also unevenly distributed. Prominent figures have teams to rebut forgeries, whereas a private individual targeted by a fabricated video may have neither the resources nor the platform access to contest it. Non-consensual synthetic imagery, in particular, falls overwhelmingly on women, and the injury persists long after a fabrication is debunked, because corrections travel more slowly than the original and rarely reach the same audience. Any serious policy must therefore consider not only the aggregate effect on public discourse but also the individuals who bear its sharpest edge. Detection offers limited comfort. Tools that identify synthetic content work by spotting statistical traces left by generators, but the generators improve in response, producing an arms race in which defenders must succeed every time and attackers only once. Moreover, a detector that is 95 per cent accurate sounds impressive until it is applied to millions of items, when it produces thousands of false accusations against authentic material. A false positive is not a trivial error; it can brand a genuine whistle-blower's video as fraudulent. A more promising line of defence is provenance: instead of asking whether a file is fake, record where it came from. Cameras and editing software can attach cryptographic signatures documenting when and by whom content was captured and what alterations followed. A viewer then learns not that the image is true, but that it carries a verifiable chain of custody. The approach has obvious limits. Signatures help only if they are widely adopted, if they survive the compression and re-uploading that content undergoes on social platforms, and if audiences learn to look for them. Content without credentials is not necessarily false, yet it may come to be treated with suspicion, burdening those who lack modern equipment, including citizen journalists in poor and conflict-ridden regions. Regulation is racing to catch up. Some jurisdictions have required labelling of synthetic content, particularly in political advertising, and others have criminalised non-consensual synthetic intimate imagery. Labelling mandates, however, bind mainly those willing to obey them; a propagandist working across borders is unlikely to attach a disclosure to a forgery. Enforcement therefore falls on platforms, which are asked to remove or flag deceptive content at enormous scale and under severe time pressure, and which face the awkward task of distinguishing satire and creative work from fraud. Overzealous removal can chill legitimate expression; insufficient removal lets damage spread before correction can arrive. Perhaps the deepest adjustment is cultural rather than technical. Societies lived for millennia without photographic evidence and developed institutions to compensate: courts that tested testimony, reputations that took years to build, and trusted intermediaries whose role was to verify before publishing. The age of synthetic media may require the return of such habits. Viewers may need to ask who is vouching for a claim rather than merely how it looks, and institutions that verify may become more valuable even as those that merely distribute become less so. None of this implies that the technology is purely harmful; the same tools lower the cost of dubbing films into dozens of languages, restoring damaged footage, and giving a voice back to patients who have lost theirs. The task is to keep these benefits while ensuring that trust, which societies build slowly and lose quickly, is not the casualty.

RC3.title: The geology of the green transition: minerals, markets and power
RC3.text: The shift from fossil fuels to clean energy is often described in the language of ideas, such as technology, innovation and ambition, but it is also a story of materials. A solar panel needs silicon, silver and copper; a wind turbine needs steel, concrete and rare-earth magnets; an electric vehicle battery needs lithium, nickel, cobalt, graphite and manganese. An electric car typically requires several times the mineral input of a conventional one, and a power grid expanded to carry renewable electricity consumes vast quantities of copper and aluminium. The transition thus replaces dependence on oil and gas with dependence on mines and refineries. The critical feature of this new dependence is not simply that these minerals are scarce, since most are geologically abundant, but that their supply is concentrated. A few countries account for most of the mining of particular metals, and a different but equally small set dominates the processing that turns raw ore into usable chemicals and alloys. Processing, in fact, is where concentration is often most severe: ore mined on one continent is frequently shipped to another for refining, which is where much of the value, and leverage, resides. A state that controls refining can influence prices and availability even when it lacks the ore itself. Concentration creates vulnerability, and vulnerability invites policy. Importing countries have responded with strategies to diversify supply: signing partnerships with resource-rich nations, subsidising domestic mining and processing, and building strategic stockpiles. Producers, for their part, have grown wary of exporting raw materials only to watch others capture the value added, and several have restricted unprocessed exports to encourage domestic refining. These moves are rational from each side's perspective, but together they risk converting commodity markets into arenas of strategic competition, with prices determined less by cost than by politics. Markets themselves complicate the picture. Mineral prices are volatile because supply responds slowly to demand: opening a mine can take a decade, while demand from battery makers can double within a few years. Price spikes encourage new investment, but by the time it arrives, demand patterns may have shifted, perhaps through a change in battery chemistry that reduces reliance on a particular metal. Cobalt illustrates the dynamic. Concern over its supply, much of which is linked to difficult working conditions, pushed manufacturers to develop cobalt-light batteries, easing the pressure but also leaving mining communities that depended on the trade exposed to a sudden fall in demand. This brings in the human and environmental costs. Mining transforms landscapes, consumes water and generates waste whose management is demanding. Communities near mines often bear the burdens while the benefits accrue elsewhere. Lithium extraction from brines, for instance, can compete with farming and herding communities for scarce water in arid regions. Abandoning fossil fuels to avert climate harm while imposing fresh harm on vulnerable communities would hollow out the moral case for the transition, and projects that lack the consent of local people have repeatedly faced delays and protests, undermining the very security of supply that governments seek. Geography adds a further layer. Deposits of many minerals lie in regions with weak institutions, and revenue from extraction can entrench conflict or corruption rather than development, the pattern often called the resource curse. Governments hoping to avoid repeating this history have begun to attach conditions to licences, requiring local processing, community benefit-sharing and transparent reporting of payments. Such conditions can raise costs and deter investors, but they may prove cheaper than the instability that follows when extraction enriches a few and burdens many. Recycling and innovation offer partial relief. Recovering metals from used batteries and electronics reduces the need for fresh mining, though the volumes available will remain small until the first large wave of batteries reaches the end of its life later this decade and beyond. Design improvements can reduce material use, and new chemistries can substitute abundant elements for scarce ones. But neither recycling nor substitution can eliminate demand in the near term; they dampen its growth rather than reverse it. The realistic path therefore combines several modest measures rather than a single decisive one: diversifying suppliers, investing in processing capacity, enforcing environmental and social standards, supporting recycling, and encouraging material-efficient designs. No single instrument is sufficient, and each carries its own trade-offs. The transition's success will depend not only on engineering but also on whether the governance of mining can be made as sophisticated as the technology it feeds.

CA1.title: Conversation: Has the common entrance test levelled the field? (Education Dialogues)
CA1.text:
CONVERSATION ANALYSIS: Read the following transcript and choose the answer that is closest to each of the questions that are based on the transcript.

Kavya Iyer (Education Correspondent): Most central universities now admit students through a single national entrance test rather than on school-board marks. Has this levelled the field, or merely changed who is tilted?

Dr. Suresh Menon (Education Policy Researcher): Both, in different measure. Board marks vary enormously in how generously they are awarded, so a common test removes one distortion. But it introduces another: access to coaching. A test that rewards drilling rewards those who can pay for drills.

Mrs. Lata Deshpande (School Principal): And it hollows out the school. Class 12 students now treat the syllabus as an obstacle between them and the entrance test. Attendance falls, and teachers lose the one lever they had, which was marks that mattered.

Dr. Suresh Menon: That is a cost, but it is not evidence against the test. It is evidence of having a test and a board exam that measure different things. If the two were aligned, the conflict would shrink.

Mrs. Lata Deshpande: Aligning them sounds neat, yet each is designed for a different purpose: one to certify a course of learning, the other to rank applicants. Merging them would damage both.

Kavya Iyer: So the choice is between two imperfect filters?

Dr. Suresh Menon: Between imperfect filters and an honest accounting of what each one filters for.

questions.question: The senator's defence was ________: it reasoned in a circle, assuming the very conclusion it purported to establish.
options: tautological
empirical
unimpeachable
inductive
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: (A) 'Tautological' describes reasoning that is circular, where the premise already contains the conclusion. (B) 'Empirical' means based on observed evidence; circular reasoning offers none. (C) 'Unimpeachable' means beyond criticism, which a circular argument is not. (D) 'Inductive' reasoning generalises from cases; it is not circular by definition.

questions.question: Although the new regulation was meant to ________ small lenders, its compliance burden fell so heavily on them that it ended up ________ the very concentration it aimed to curb.
options: penalise; reducing
empower; dispersing
regulate; forestalling
shield; entrenching
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: (A) 'Penalise' contradicts 'meant to'; also 'reducing' concentration contradicts the outcome implied by 'ended up'. (B) If the rule empowered small lenders and dispersed concentration, there would be no irony; 'although' signals a failure. (C) 'Forestalling' concentration is the aim, not the unintended result. (D) The intent was to protect small lenders ('shield'), but costs on them pushed business to large players, 'entrenching' concentration.

questions.question: The mayor's ________ response to the crisis, dithering until events forced his hand, contrasted sharply with his deputy's ________ decisiveness.
options: impetuous; reckless
irresolute; unwavering
circumspect; precipitate
prompt; swift
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: (A) 'Impetuous' is the opposite of dithering. (B) 'Irresolute' fits 'dithering'; 'unwavering' reinforces 'decisiveness' as a contrast. (C) 'Circumspect' suggests careful caution, and 'precipitate' (hasty) does not fit 'decisiveness' as praise; weaker on both blanks. (D) 'Prompt' contradicts 'dithering'.

questions.question: Having squandered the goodwill of her allies through repeated ________, the negotiator found herself isolated when ________ was most needed.
options: magnanimity; confrontation
diligence; compromise
duplicity; solidarity
candour; consensus
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: (A) 'Magnanimity' (generosity) would not squander goodwill. (B) 'Diligence' is a virtue and does not squander goodwill. (C) Repeated deceit ('duplicity') destroys goodwill, leaving her without 'solidarity' when it counted. (D) 'Candour' (honesty) would build, not destroy, goodwill.

questions.question: In the sentence 'His mercurial temperament made him a difficult colleague, since no one could predict how he would respond from one day to the next', the word 'mercurial' most nearly means:
options: calm and consistent under sustained pressure from colleagues
quick to forgive those who have wronged him in the past
sharply intelligent but emotionally withdrawn from others
prone to sudden, unpredictable change
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: (A) The opposite: the sentence says nobody could predict his response. (B) Forgiveness is not mentioned or implied. (C) Intelligence and withdrawal are not implied; the sentence is about unpredictability. (D) 'Mercurial' (like the volatile planet or metal) means subject to sudden, unpredictable shifts of mood.

questions.question: In 'The review was fulsome in its praise, and readers distrusted it', 'fulsome' most nearly means:
options: excessive to the point of insincerity
generous and warmly deserved in every respect
brief and carefully understated in tone
reluctant and grudging in expression
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: (A) 'Fulsome' means excessive, often cloying and insincere; that is why readers distrusted it. (B) Common misreading: 'fulsome' is often mistaken for 'full' and generous. (C) Understatement would not provoke distrust here. (D) 'Grudging' contradicts 'praise'.

questions.question: Choose the word most nearly OPPOSITE in meaning to 'munificent'.
options: benevolent
prodigal
miserly
affluent
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: (A) 'Benevolent' is a synonym, not an opposite. (B) 'Prodigal' means wastefully extravagant: related to spending, but not the opposite of generosity. (C) 'Munificent' means very generous; 'miserly' means unwilling to give or spend. (D) 'Affluent' means wealthy; wealth is not the same as generosity.

questions.question: Which of the following best explains the expression 'to cross the Rubicon'?
options: To abandon a long-standing alliance in the face of mounting pressure
To take a step from which there is no turning back
To succeed by a narrow margin after a prolonged struggle
To cross a boundary with the intention of attacking a rival
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: (A) Describes betrayal of an alliance, unrelated to irrevocability. (B) Caesar's crossing of the Rubicon with his army committed him irrevocably to civil war. (C) Describes a narrow win, unrelated to the idiom. (D) Close to the literal event but misses the sense of an irreversible commitment.

questions.question: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
options: The number of applicants have risen, but a number of them lacks the required qualifications.
The number of applicants has risen, but a number of them lacks the required qualifications.
The number of applicants has risen, but a number of them lack the required qualifications.
The number of applicants have risen, but a number of them lack the required qualifications.
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: (A) Both verbs are wrong: 'the number' needs 'has', and 'a number of them' needs 'lack'. (B) First verb is right, but 'a number of them' is plural and needs 'lack'. (C) 'The number' is singular (has); 'a number of' is plural (lack). (D) 'Applicants' is not the subject; 'the number' is, so it needs 'has'.

questions.question: Choose the sentence that is correct and parallel in structure.
options: The proposal aims at reducing costs, improving quality and expanding access.
The proposal aims at reducing costs, improving quality, and to expand access.
The proposal aims to reduce costs, improving quality, and expanding access.
The proposal aims at reducing costs, to improve quality, and expanding access.
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: (A) All three items are gerunds after 'aims at'. (B) Final item switches to an infinitive, breaking parallelism. (C) First item is an infinitive while the other two are gerunds. (D) Middle item is an infinitive in a list of gerunds.

questions.question: Not only the students but also the principal ________ concerned about the new policy.
options: are
is
have been
were being
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: (A) Would be correct if the nearer subject were plural. (B) With 'not only... but also', the verb agrees with the nearer subject ('the principal', singular). (C) Plural and tense do not match the present-tense context. (D) Plural and an unnatural progressive; no agreement with 'principal'.

questions.question: One of the sentences below contains a word used incorrectly or inappropriately. Choose that sentence.
options: The orator's sonorous voice carried to the very last row of the vast amphitheatre.
Her magnanimous gesture, forgiving a rival who had slandered her, surprised the whole audience.
The findings were so unequivocal that they left considerable room for doubt.
The firm's sanguine projections were vindicated when profits reached a record high.
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: (A) 'Sonorous' (deep and resonant) is used correctly. (B) 'Magnanimous' (generous in forgiving) is used correctly. (C) 'Unequivocal' means leaving no doubt, which contradicts 'room for doubt'. The intended word is 'equivocal' or 'ambiguous'. (D) 'Sanguine' (optimistic) is used correctly.

questions.question: One of the sentences below contains a word used incorrectly or inappropriately. Choose that sentence.
options: His fastidious attention to detail meant that errors routinely slipped through unnoticed.
The judge's disinterested ruling, free of any personal stake, was praised by both parties.
The tycoon's ostentatious mansion, with its gilded gates, drew the envy of the neighbourhood.
The candidate's pragmatic approach favoured workable compromises over ideological purity.
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: (A) 'Fastidious' means meticulous, which contradicts errors slipping through. The intended word is 'cursory' or 'lax'. (B) 'Disinterested' (impartial) is used correctly. (C) 'Ostentatious' (showy) is used correctly. (D) 'Pragmatic' (practical) is used correctly.

questions.question: One of the sentences below contains a word used incorrectly or inappropriately. Choose that sentence.
options: The sceptic's scathing review left the playwright visibly shaken by its severity.
The village's insular customs had changed little in centuries of relative isolation.
The plan's viability depended on the cooperation of several wary stakeholders.
The committee's judicious decision to ignore the evidence surprised observers.
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: (A) 'Scathing' (harshly critical) is used correctly. (B) 'Insular' (isolated, narrow) is used correctly. (C) 'Viability' (feasibility) is used correctly. (D) 'Judicious' means showing good judgement, which contradicts ignoring all evidence. The intended word is 'injudicious' or 'perverse'.

questions.question: Attention has become the scarcest resource in the digital economy. ____________. A feed that never ends, a notification timed to the moment of greatest vulnerability, and an autoplay countdown that removes the decision to stop are all engineering choices. To call the resulting behaviour a 'lack of willpower' is to ignore who built the temptation.
options: Most users report that they spend less time on their devices than they did five years earlier.
Governments have allocated significant funding to schools for teaching digital skills to young people everywhere.
Platforms compete for it, and many design choices are calibrated to capture it rather than serve the user.
Advertising revenue has declined in most major markets as consumers shift to subscription-based services entirely.
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: (A) Contradicts the sense of rising capture; not supported. (B) Shifts to education funding, which the paragraph never mentions. (C) Sets up the 'engineering choices' that follow and the blame placed on builders. (D) Introduces an advertising claim that is irrelevant to the argument.

questions.question: Inflation is often reported as a single number, but it is experienced as many. ____________. A household spending most of its income on food and fuel faces a rate far removed from the one the average basket suggests. Policy aimed at the headline figure can therefore miss the people it is meant to protect.
options: Central banks have lowered interest rates in most large economies during the last several years of slow growth.
Economists agree that moderate inflation is preferable to deflation in nearly every historical circumstance observed.
Wages in most sectors have grown faster than prices, leaving workers better off than they were a decade ago.
Price rises are unevenly spread across goods, and households weight those goods very differently.
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: (A) About interest rates; unrelated. (B) About the desirability of inflation; unrelated to its unequal incidence. (C) A claim about wages that contradicts the paragraph's concern about unprotected households. (D) Leads into the household-level contrast in the next sentence.

questions.question: Cities do not merely grow; they accrete. ____________. A medieval lane survives beneath a colonial boulevard, which in turn lies beneath a modern flyover, and each layer constrains what the next can become. Planners who imagine a blank slate soon find that the past has a veto.
options: Modern cities are growing faster than at any other time in human history, particularly in Asia and Africa.
Each generation builds on, around and often over the decisions of the ones before it.
Flyovers reduce congestion in the short term but rarely improve the long-term quality of urban life.
Colonial architecture has been carefully preserved in most cities because of its aesthetic value to visitors.
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: (A) About growth rates; the paragraph is about layering. (B) Introduces layering, which the lane–boulevard–flyover example illustrates. (C) About flyovers' effects, a minor detail in the example. (D) About preservation, which the paragraph does not address.

questions.question:
Which of the following best summarises the paragraph?

Scientific journals reward novelty, and a result that merely confirms an established finding is rarely published. Consequently, studies that fail to replicate seldom appear in print, while surprising findings, some of them statistical flukes, attract attention and citations. The literature thus overrepresents positive results, and a reader who surveys it may conclude that a weak effect is strong.
options: Replication studies are unreliable because they are usually conducted by less experienced researchers than the original authors.
Statistical flukes are the main reason that scientific findings are rejected by journals that value novelty above accuracy.
Readers should avoid surveying the literature because published studies are written to attract citations rather than to inform.
Journals' taste for novelty skews the published record towards positive findings, inflating apparent effects.
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: (A) The paragraph says nothing about researchers' experience. (B) Reverses the causation: flukes are rewarded, not rejected. (C) Overreaches: the author warns readers about bias, not about reading at all. (D) Captures the chain: novelty reward → non-replications unpublished → inflated picture.

questions.question: Three of the following four sentences relate to a common theme. Choose the sentence that does not belong.
options: The ministry announced revised guidelines for the construction of rural roads.
Monthly SIP inflows reached a record as retail investors steadily raised their contributions.
Equity mutual funds drew fresh inflows even as benchmark indices consolidated.
Assets managed by fund houses crossed another milestone this quarter.
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: (A) It concerns infrastructure policy; the others describe mutual fund flows and assets. (B) Mutual fund flows. (C) Mutual fund flows. (D) Mutual fund assets.

questions.question:
The five sentences (labelled 1-5) given below, when arranged in the correct order, form a coherent paragraph. Enter the correct sequence of the numbers as your answer.

1. Trees lower street temperatures, reduce energy spent on cooling and raise the value of adjoining property.
2. Such benefits accrue to those who never pay for them, which is why private developers rarely provide green space unprompted.
3. Parks are usually defended on aesthetic grounds, as places of beauty and rest.
4. Public provision, therefore, is less a luxury than a correction to a market failure.
5. Their economic role is less often acknowledged.
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: Sentence 3 introduces the usual defence. Sentence 5 ('Their economic role') pivots. Sentence 1 lists the economic benefits. Sentence 2 ('Such benefits') shows who captures them. Sentence 4 ('therefore') concludes. Order: 3-5-1-2-4.

questions.question:
The five sentences (labelled 1-5) given below, when arranged in the correct order, form a coherent paragraph. Enter the correct sequence of the numbers as your answer.

1. Verifying that counterfactual is difficult, since no one can observe the forest that would have been felled without the project.
2. Carbon credits were designed to let those who can cut emissions cheaply do so on behalf of those who cannot.
3. A market that cannot tell genuine reductions from imagined ones rewards the cheapest claims, not the best.
4. The logic holds only if each credit represents a reduction that would not otherwise have occurred.
5. Buyers consequently face credits of widely varying integrity, priced almost identically.
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: Sentence 2 states the design. Sentence 4 gives the condition. Sentence 1 ('that counterfactual') explains the verification problem. Sentence 5 ('consequently') gives the effect on buyers. Sentence 3 concludes. Order: 2-4-1-5-3.

questions.question:
The five sentences (labelled 1-5) given below, when arranged in the correct order, form a coherent paragraph. Enter the correct sequence of the numbers as your answer.

1. Stability, however, can breed dependence, as local economies may come to rely on a flow that policy cannot control.
2. Unlike investment, they flow directly into households, where they fund consumption, schooling and housing.
3. The challenge is to convert a safety net into a springboard.
4. Remittances now rival foreign investment as a source of external finance for several developing economies.
5. This directness makes them remarkably stable, since migrants tend to send more home when their families face hardship.
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: Sentence 4 introduces remittances. Sentence 2 ('Unlike investment') contrasts. Sentence 5 ('This directness') follows. Sentence 1 ('Stability, however') adds the risk. Sentence 3 concludes. Order: 4-2-5-1-3.

questions.question:
The five sentences (labelled 1-5) given below, when arranged in the correct order, form a coherent paragraph. Enter the correct sequence of the numbers as your answer.

1. The yardstick, once adopted, begins to shape what it was meant merely to measure.
2. Standardised tests promise a common yardstick in a system where schools differ widely in quality.
3. But comparability is bought at the price of narrowness, since only what can be measured on paper enters the yardstick.
4. Teachers consequently orient instruction towards the test, and skills that resist measurement quietly recede.
5. Their appeal lies in comparability: a score in one city means the same as a score in another.
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: Sentence 2 introduces the tests. Sentence 5 ('Their appeal') explains why. Sentence 3 ('But') shows the cost. Sentence 4 ('consequently') gives the effect. Sentence 1 concludes. Order: 2-5-3-4-1.

questions.question:
The five sentences (labelled 1-5) given below, when arranged in the correct order, form a coherent paragraph. Enter the correct sequence of the numbers as your answer.

1. Overuse selects for resistant bacteria, which then spread beyond the settings where they arose.
2. Their very success encouraged overuse, in clinics and on farms alike.
3. The market that gave us the cure thus struggles to protect it.
4. Antibiotics transformed medicine by making routine surgery and childbirth survivable.
5. Developing replacement drugs is commercially unattractive, since a new antibiotic is best held in reserve and therefore sells little.
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: Sentence 4 introduces antibiotics. Sentence 2 ('Their very success') follows. Sentence 1 explains the consequence of overuse. Sentence 5 explains why replacements are scarce. Sentence 3 ('thus') concludes. Order: 4-2-1-5-3.

questions.question: On which of the following do Dr. Menon and Mrs. Deshpande disagree?
options: Whether coaching gives wealthier students an advantage in entrance tests
Whether the two examinations could be usefully aligned
Whether a common test removes distortions arising from uneven board marking
Whether schools suffer when students prioritise the entrance test over the syllabus
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: (A) Only Menon raises coaching; Deshpande never disputes it. (B) Menon thinks alignment would reduce the conflict; Deshpande says merging would damage both. (C) Menon says so; Deshpande does not dispute it. (D) Menon concedes this is a cost; there is no disagreement.

questions.question: Dr. Menon's remark that the hollowing-out of schools 'is not evidence against the test' implies that, in his view:
options: the decline in attendance is exaggerated by principals who oppose entrance examinations as a matter of principle
schools should be compensated by the state for losses suffered as a result of the national entrance test
board examinations should be abolished because they cannot be reconciled with the purpose of an entrance test
schools' decline stems from misaligned assessments, not common testing itself
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: (A) He accepts that it is a real cost, not exaggerated. (B) He proposes no compensation. (C) He proposes alignment, not abolition. (D) He attributes the conflict to the two exams measuring different things, so aligning them would reduce it.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT stated or implied by Mrs. Deshpande?
options: Teachers' leverage has weakened because marks matter less than the entrance score.
Class 12 students regard the school syllabus as a hindrance to their preparation.
Coaching institutes should be regulated.
Board exams and entrance tests serve different purposes.
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: (A) Implied: teachers lose 'the one lever they had'. (B) Stated explicitly. (C) She never discusses regulation; coaching is mentioned only by Menon. (D) Stated explicitly: certify learning versus rank applicants.

questions.question: Which of the following best captures the central argument of the passage?
options: Local-currency settlement will soon dethrone the dollar, since sanctions have convinced most governments that its dominance is unsustainable.
De-dollarisation should be abandoned because fragmented currencies raise transaction costs more than dollar dependence ever has done.
Reducing dollar dependence is desirable but difficult, and is likely to advance gradually through institutional groundwork.
India should immediately open its capital account fully so that the rupee can compete with the dollar as a reserve currency.
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: (A) The author predicts diversification rather than dethronement, so 'soon dethrone' is wrong. (B) Fragmentation is a cost the author notes, but the author does not call for abandonment. (C) Matches the final paragraph and the 'gradual diversification at the margin' view. (D) The author warns that convertibility is double-edged and recommends incremental steps.

questions.question: According to the passage, why have some local-currency trade arrangements struggled?
options: Exporters were left holding balances they could neither convert freely nor use productively.
Importing partners refused to accept the currency for invoicing because sanctions laws prohibit any payment in non-dollar currencies.
Central banks involved withheld swap lines in order to protect their own exchange rates from any speculative pressure.
Both trading partners preferred to settle in dollars because dollar invoicing eliminates exchange-rate risk entirely for them.
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: (A) Stated in paragraph 3 as the 'idle balances' problem. (B) Sanctions laws are not said to prohibit non-dollar payment. (C) The passage does not mention central banks withholding swap lines. (D) The passage says dollar invoicing exposes parties to exchange-rate swings, not that it eliminates risk.

questions.question: Which of the following can be inferred from paragraph 4?
options: Balanced bilateral trade removes the need for any supporting financial infrastructure such as swap lines or rupee-denominated bonds.
Lopsided trade can always be settled smoothly in the currency of whichever country exports more to the other.
Third-currency settlement is cheaper and more reliable than direct settlement in either partner's local currency.
Surplus partners will accumulate the importer's currency unless they can spend or invest it.
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: (A) The passage says balanced trade is settled with 'little friction', not that infrastructure is unnecessary. (B) The passage says lopsided trade cannot be settled without friction. (C) A third currency 'brings the dollar straight back in'; the passage does not call it cheaper. (D) Follows directly from the discussion of lopsided trade.

questions.question: The 'paradox' mentioned in paragraph 5 refers to the fact that:
options: currencies grow more valuable when governments restrict their use, yet restrictions are removed as the currency becomes more valuable.
gaining autonomy from the dollar may require surrendering some control over capital flows.
countries that avoid sanctions risk become targets of sanctions because their trade is settled outside the dollar system.
a currency attracts foreign investors only when it is not freely convertible, yet convertibility is the stated goal of policy.
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: (A) The passage makes no such claim about restrictions and value. (B) Paragraph 5 says internationalisation demands surrendering control, the thing that motivated the exercise. (C) The passage does not claim that sanctions target such countries. (D) The passage says convertibility invites investment, not that it deters it.

questions.question: All of the following are mentioned as reasons governments are interested in de-dollarisation EXCEPT:
options: higher returns on reserves held abroad
exposure to exchange-rate swings unrelated to domestic conditions
lower transaction costs and shorter settlement chains
insulation of trade from the risk of sanctions
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: (A) Never mentioned in the passage. (B) Mentioned in paragraph 2. (C) Mentioned in paragraph 2. (D) Mentioned in paragraph 2.

questions.question: The author's attitude toward de-dollarisation is best described as:
options: enthusiastically optimistic that the dollar's dominance will end within a few years as alternatives mature.
dismissive of the whole project, treating it as political posturing without any possible economic benefit.
cautiously sceptical of rapid change, yet supportive of gradual, institution-based reform.
indifferent to the outcome, presenting the arguments for and against without favouring any approach at all.
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: (A) Contradicts 'gradual diversification' and the cautionary tone. (B) The author acknowledges real motives and benefits. (C) Reflected in the cautious tone and the incremental recommendation for India. (D) The author does recommend an incremental approach.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the main point of the passage?
options: Detection tools will eventually defeat synthetic media, making regulation and changes in social habits largely unnecessary.
Synthetic media erodes trust in all evidence, and defences must combine provenance, regulation and cultural change.
Synthetic media is harmful on balance and should be banned, since its legitimate uses cannot offset the damage it causes.
Fabricated recordings are mainly a problem for politicians, since ordinary citizens are rarely targeted by voice cloning or forgery.
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: (A) The passage calls detection limited, not conclusive. (B) Summarises the problem (paras 1-2) and the layered responses (paras 4-6). (C) The passage says the technology is not purely harmful and does not call for a ban. (D) Ordinary people are cited as targets (cloned voice persuading a relative).

questions.question: As used in the passage, the 'liar's dividend' refers to the fact that:
options: firms that sell detection tools to governments and platforms profit heavily during election periods.
forgers gain a reputational benefit when their fabricated recordings are mistaken for authentic footage.
audiences benefit when synthetic content lowers the cost of dubbing and restoring footage.
genuine evidence can be dismissed as fake by those it incriminates.
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: (A) Profits of detection firms are never discussed. (B) Reputational gains for forgers are not what the term describes. (C) Dubbing and restoration are benefits mentioned in the last paragraph, a different point. (D) Paragraph 2 defines it: a wrongdoer can claim the tape is synthetic.

questions.question: Which of the following can be inferred about detection tools from the passage?
options: A seemingly accurate detector can still wrongly flag many authentic items at scale.
Detection tools are useless, since generators will always improve faster than any defender can possibly respond.
Accuracy figures of ninety-five per cent are routinely exaggerated by developers of detection software seeking contracts.
False positives matter less than false negatives, because authentic material is rarely subjected to detection at all.
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: (A) Follows from the 95 per cent example applied to millions of items. (B) The passage calls detection of limited comfort, not useless. (C) No claim is made about developers exaggerating accuracy. (D) The passage treats false positives as serious, not minor.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken provenance signatures as a defence against synthetic media?
options: Cryptographic signatures can be attached by cameras at the moment of capture without any special action by the photographer.
Several major camera manufacturers have announced that they will include signing features in their newest models.
Most viewers never check credentials, and platforms routinely strip signatures when content is shared.
Citizen journalists in conflict regions increasingly use modern devices capable of attaching provenance records to their footage.
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: (A) Makes provenance easier, so it strengthens the defence. (B) Indicates growing adoption, so it strengthens the defence. (C) Undermines both adoption and survival of signatures, the passage's stated conditions for success. (D) Reduces the burden on citizen journalists, so it strengthens the defence.

questions.question: All of the following are mentioned as difficulties with regulating synthetic media EXCEPT:
options: Labelling mandates bind mainly those willing to comply with them.
Courts lack the technical expertise to authenticate digital evidence.
Platforms must distinguish satire and creative work from fraud under time pressure.
Overzealous removal of content can chill legitimate expression.
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: (A) Mentioned in paragraph 5. (B) Not mentioned in the passage. (C) Mentioned in paragraph 5. (D) Mentioned in paragraph 5.

questions.question: The author's reference to societies that lived without photographic evidence serves mainly to:
options: argue that photographic evidence was never reliable and should not have been trusted even in the twentieth century
show that societies without recorded evidence were more honest and less prone to deception than modern ones
claim that courts and reputations are more resilient against forgery than any technological safeguard that exists today
suggest that older institutions of verification may regain importance
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: (A) The author does not claim photographs were never reliable. (B) No claim of greater honesty is made. (C) The author does not rank institutions above technology. (D) Paragraph 6 argues that habits such as trusted intermediaries may need to return.

questions.question: Which of the following best states the central argument of the passage?
options: The green transition creates new mineral dependencies whose risks call for a mix of modest measures.
Mineral scarcity will make the green transition impossible unless nations agree to halt extraction in all environmentally sensitive regions.
Recycling and substitution can end mineral dependence within a decade, making supplier diversification and standards unnecessary.
Producer nations should be prevented from restricting exports of unprocessed ore because such restrictions undermine global supply chains.
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: (A) Reflects the opening, the vulnerability argument and the closing recommendation. (B) The passage says most minerals are geologically abundant, so scarcity is not the core issue. (C) The passage says recycling and substitution only dampen demand growth. (D) The author calls producers' moves 'rational' and does not advocate preventing them.

questions.question: According to the passage, why does control over processing give a state leverage?
options: Processing requires technology that no country other than a few advanced economies is capable of acquiring or developing.
Refined minerals are scarcer geologically than raw ores, which gives their producers a natural monopoly over supply and prices.
Much of the value and control lies in refining, so refiners can sway supply even without ore.
Importers prefer to buy refined products because shipping unprocessed ore across continents is prohibitively expensive and damaging.
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: (A) The passage does not claim processing technology is unattainable. (B) The passage says most minerals are geologically abundant, not scarce. (C) Paragraph 2 says a state controlling refining can influence prices and availability even when it lacks the ore. (D) Shipping costs are not discussed as the reason.

questions.question: The cobalt example in the passage illustrates that:
options: high prices for a mineral invariably lead to a permanent increase in mining employment in the producing regions.
price pressure can spur substitution that eases supply worries while harming dependent communities.
technological substitution is impossible for minerals whose supply is concentrated in a few politically unstable countries.
concern about working conditions in mining reduces global demand for batteries and thereby slows the clean-energy transition.
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: (A) The example shows the opposite of 'invariably'. (B) Cobalt-light batteries eased pressure but left mining communities exposed to a demand fall. (C) The example shows substitution is possible. (D) The example concerns cobalt demand, not demand for batteries overall.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would best support the claim that projects lacking local consent can undermine security of supply?
options: Governments in several mineral-rich countries have increased their share of mining revenues by renegotiating contracts with foreign firms.
Mining companies that invested in community programmes reported higher profit margins than those that did not do so.
New refining plants have been commissioned at a faster pace than new mines in most importing countries recently.
A major lithium project was suspended for years after local communities contested water allocation.
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: (A) Concerns revenue sharing, not consent or supply disruption. (B) Suggests community engagement pays but does not show supply being undermined without it. (C) Concerns the pace of refining versus mining, which is unrelated to consent. (D) A direct example of consent problems causing delay and loss of supply.

questions.question: All of the following are measures the author recommends EXCEPT:
options: imposing a global ban on exports of unprocessed ore.
investing in processing capacity at home or among partners.
enforcing environmental and social standards in mining.
encouraging designs that use materials more efficiently.
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: (A) Not recommended; the passage describes export restrictions only as a producer response with risks. (B) Recommended in the last paragraph. (C) Recommended in the last paragraph. (D) Recommended in the last paragraph.

questions.question: The tone of the passage is best described as:
options: alarmist, warning that civilisation faces imminent collapse unless extraction is halted immediately everywhere.
triumphant, celebrating the transition as an unqualified success that is now beyond any realistic risk.
analytical and measured, wary of any single remedy.
cynical, suggesting that governments and companies have no genuine interest in solving the problems described.
questions.explanation: Detailed Solution: (A) No language of imminent collapse. (B) The author acknowledges risks, so it is not triumphant. (C) The passage weighs trade-offs and rejects a single decisive instrument. (D) The author calls moves 'rational' and recommends workable measures; no cynicism.

words.meaning: saying the same thing twice in different words; circular in logic
words.example: 'The law is the law' is a tautological defence.

words.meaning: subject to sudden, unpredictable changes of mood
words.example: Her mercurial temper unsettled the team.

words.meaning: excessive, especially in a way that seems insincere

words.example: A munificent donor funded the new library.
His duplicity cost him every ally.

words.meaning: hesitant; unable to make up one's mind
words.example: The irresolute board delayed the decision again.

words.meaning: done suddenly and without careful thought (adj.); to bring about abruptly (v.)
words.example: A precipitate cut in rates unsettled markets.

words.meaning: the origin or chain of custody of something
words.example: The painting's provenance was carefully documented.

words.meaning: dominance of one state or group over others
words.example: The dollar's hegemony is being quietly tested.
The firm's insular culture resisted outside ideas.

idioms.example: Signing the merger deal meant crossing the Rubicon.

idioms.meaning: a small visible part of a much larger problem
idioms.example: The audit revealed only the tip of the iceberg.

idioms.meaning: a situation where one side's gain equals the other's loss
idioms.example: Critics treat trade as a zero-sum game.
Regulation aims to create a level playing field.
The new entrant threw down the gauntlet to incumbents.

phrasal_verbs.example: The deal fell through at the last minute.

phrasal_verbs.meaning: to support; to make a copy
phrasal_verbs.example: The data backs up her claim.

phrasal_verbs.meaning: to join a discussion with an opinion
phrasal_verbs.example: Economists weighed in on the budget.
The minister ruled out any rate cut.
